Yup, very much so. I'm an old (literally) missile guy. We had a command and control test set for lack of a better description that used a punch card reader. We'd cable it up and run reams of punch cards thru it in a sequence that was an end to end test of the system. Would take over a day, sometimes two, feeding a card, waiting for results ... onto next card - LOL. In another example, we also always got chewed out for not filing 'paperwork' correctly, because the key punch operators couldn't decipher it when cutting the cards for entry into the 'system' that tracked maintenance operations. Those were the days.

My first programming class required making punch cards, submitting the deck of cards to the computer center which only ran student jobs at night, returning the next morning to find you made one typo that bombed the job.
I remember for student programmers it was the old compile and go routine. Then go for coffee while you waited for the printout results.

They stayed around longer than you might think. I played with them as a child in the early 80's, and then had to work with them as a teenager in the 90's. The last time I saw an active IBM 3505 was in 1998. It was a huge metal monster, roughly the size of two refrigerators, connected to an AS/400 that was only slightly larger than a modern desktop PC.
You always realized you forgot to number them right after you dropped the whole stack.
